target_audience: general public, seekers, students of philosophy and literature
book_summary: Why man is great. A frame-story novel that asks the oldest question of the Baul, the Fakir, the Udasi, the Vairagi, and the home-leaver: what makes a human being great? Not wealth, not caste, not name, not power — but the inward journey of leaving the false house and finding the person of the heart. Each chapter is a workshop where a modern gathering hears a narrated story of a seeker who walks the road without owning it, practices without claiming the fruit, and loves without chaining the beloved.

chapters.name: Introduction
chapters.chapter_summary: The opening workshop frames the central question: why is man great? A modern gathering of seekers, artists, and skeptics meets to hear the first story. The narrator introduces the figure of the Gosai — the traveler who leaves home to find the deeper home under the open sky. The first story plants the seed: greatness is not in what a person owns, but in what a person is willing to leave behind.

chapters.name: Chapter 1
chapters.chapter_summary: The story of the Baul — the wind-touched wanderer whose divine restlessness breaks social chains. The workshop characters debate whether madness can be wisdom. The narrated story follows a Baul who leaves caste and creed to seek the person of the heart, and in doing so reveals the first measure of human greatness: the courage to be free.

chapters.name: Chapter 2
chapters.chapter_summary: The story of the Fakir — the poor one whose poverty is not lack but release. The workshop characters confront their own attachment to wealth and status. The narrated story follows a Fakir who wants nothing except freedom from wanting, and reveals the second measure of greatness: the lightness of a heart that owns nothing.

chapters.name: Chapter 3
chapters.chapter_summary: The story of the Udasi — the unattached one who walks the road without claiming it. The workshop characters wrestle with the meaning of belonging. The narrated story follows an Udasi who loves without turning love into possession, and reveals the third measure of greatness: the blade that cuts false bondage.

chapters.name: Chapter 4
chapters.chapter_summary: The story of the Vairagi — the one who has turned away from worldly attachment. The workshop characters question whether detachment is sorrow or clarity. The narrated story follows a Vairagi who wishes to wake from the dream of the world, and reveals the fourth measure of greatness: the clarity that sees the world as it is.

chapters.name: Chapter 5
chapters.chapter_summary: The story of the home-leaver — the traveler who does not mistake shelter for truth. The workshop characters reflect on their own false houses: pride, name, possession, caste, fear, habit. The narrated story follows a home-leaver whose true departure is inward, and reveals the fifth measure of greatness: the inward turn.

chapters.name: Chapter 6
chapters.chapter_summary: The story of the road — discipline, uncertainty, dust, weather, and song. The workshop characters learn that the path itself is the end. The narrated story follows a traveler who discovers there is no fixed destination, and reveals the sixth measure of greatness: the willingness to walk without a map.

chapters.name: Chapter 7
chapters.chapter_summary: The story of the song of the road — sung by those who walk, carrying dust, wind, shade, longing, and freedom. The workshop characters hear the song and are moved. The narrated story follows a singer who lives in the act of singing, and reveals the seventh measure of greatness: the freedom that does not seek permanence.

chapters.name: Chapter 8
chapters.chapter_summary: The story of the person of the heart — the hidden self, the beloved truth within each human being. The workshop characters turn inward. The narrated story follows a seeker who leaves the false house of society's mask and inherited identity, and reveals the eighth measure of greatness: the discovery of the inner beloved.

chapters.name: Conclusion
chapters.chapter_title: শেষ কথা: যে কথা শেষ হয় না
chapters.chapter_summary: The closing workshop gathers all the figures — Baul, Fakir, Udasi, Vairagi, and home-leaver — into one figure: the Gosai. The final story reveals the last word that ends all words and yet remains inexhaustible. The answer to 'why man is great' is spoken and left open: man is great because he can walk without owning the path, practice without claiming the fruit, and love without chaining the beloved.
